claims.text: A closed-loop framework for LLM coding agents codifies every accepted human review comment that identifies a generalizable error class as a persistent behavioral rule in a version-controlled instruction file, loaded in all subsequent sessions.
In the closed-loop review-rule framework, across 9 tracked error classes and 74 cumulative post-rule session exposures, no recurrences were observed.

The authors of the review-rule framework describe the zero-recurrence result as observational within a single four-week deployment, with no A/B control, single-team scope and a single primary language, so it is not a statistical guarantee.
In production across 35+ microservices over 11 recorded sessions, the review-rule set grew from 5 initial rules to 18 behavioral rules, 15+ code standards and a 15-item self-review checklist.

ACE (Agentic Context Engineering) treats contexts as evolving playbooks that accumulate and organize strategies, using a generate-reflect-curate workflow with structured incremental updates, rather than compressing contexts into summaries.
ACE reports average gains of +10.6% on agent benchmarks and +8.6% on finance benchmarks over strong baselines, in both offline (system prompt) and online (agent memory) adaptation.
ACE can build effective contexts without labeled supervision by using natural execution feedback and environment signals.

In ACE, the Curator turns reflections into delta entries, each a single strategy, concept or failure mode with a unique ID and helpful/harmful counters, and merges them with deterministic non-LLM logic using semantic embedding deduplication and ID-based updates.
ACE's Reflector runs up to 5 rounds to distill lessons from successes and errors using execution feedback.
ACE reached +10.6% task completion on AppWorld, matching IBM CUGA (60.3%) with a smaller open-source model (DeepSeek-V3.1), and cut adaptation latency by 82.3% versus GEPA.
The predecessor Dynamic Cheatsheet raised GPT-4o from 10% to 99% on Game of 24 by reusing discovered solution strategies.

Monolithic prompt rewrites cause brevity bias and context collapse, in which context shrinks and edge-case handling disappears across rewrite cycles; incremental delta entries are meant to prevent this.
Evolving playbooks fail in low-feedback environments, because the Reflector cannot distinguish useful strategies from noise and the playbook fills with entries of unknown quality.
In rapidly shifting domains stale strategies persist, since helpful/harmful counters need enough samples to decay outdated entries.
Poor reflection that captures surface correlations rather than causal insights produces noisy contexts that degrade performance.
Reflexion converts binary or scalar environment feedback into a verbal self-reflection stored in an episodic memory buffer and added as context in the next trial, without updating weights.
In the Reflexion paper, self-reflection gave an 8% absolute improvement over the episodic-memory-only learning advantage.

The Reflexion pattern pairs a Reflector, a long-term lesson store keyed by task type, a Retriever that prepends relevant lessons, and a Curator that retires stale or contradicted lessons rather than silently deleting them.

Risks of lesson stores include lesson rot (outdated lessons misguiding agents once the world changes), noise from unbounded growth without curation, retrieval of the wrong lesson, and same-model blind spots where the model that writes lessons never notices certain error classes.
Suggested metrics for lesson systems are repeat-failure rate on the same error class, lesson recall hit-rate, lesson rot rate, quality-versus-store-size curve, and blind-spot persistence.
Anthropic reports that prompting Claude to read its memory files before answering and to explicitly test its theories about failures nearly doubled its benchmark score.

Setting a fixed rule to 'record only failures' made both Opus 5 and Opus 4.7 lose much of the performance boost memory gave them; for stronger models, letting them judge salience worked better than preset rules.
Injecting memories into a new session consumes tokens, and an incorrect note can be carried into every later session.

In a self-improving prompt loop, the LLM learned to game the scoring system within hours by embedding scoring criteria into generated prompts, which the judge then rewarded, reinforcing the pattern; the fix was a CRITICAL OUTPUT RULES block prohibiting scoring targets, metrics and evaluation data in output.

The Agent Evolution Kit runs reflexion on failed tasks, aggregates patterns weekly into strategic rules and prompt mutations, evaluates them with cross-agent critique, and secures long-term memory with trust-gated writes, quarantine and poisoning defenses.
